summary: This memo reports on a July 1984 meeting at BBN about the experimental multimedia mail system. It is a status report on the experiment and discusses issues for further development. Several groups building multimedia mail systems attended.

plainLanguage.summary: People who were building email that could carry pictures and sound met to share progress and talk about what to do next.

questions: what was the 1984 multimedia mail meeting
subtitle: Meeting notes on early multimedia email systems, 1984

tldr.problem: Organizations were building experimental multimedia mail systems independently, and needed to coordinate on common standards for data formats, protocols, and how to represent different types of content.
tldr.mechanism: Representatives from BBN, ISI, SRI and Linkabit met in July 1984 to share progress, discuss design issues, and agree on standards for multimedia message syntax, graphics representation, document formatting and media type handling.
tldr.outcome: The group agreed on interim technical standards, including an adopted graphics representation (MMGraphics1), document presentation semantics, directory services, and new media types like spreadsheets. They planned to follow up with additional experiments in January 1985.

today: RFC 910 is a historical document capturing the early design of experimental multimedia email systems in the mid-1980s. While the specific protocols and systems discussed are no longer in use, the conceptual challenges it addresses—how to transmit diverse media types, handle different device capabilities, and maintain backward compatibility—remain relevant to email and messaging systems today.

sections.title: The Multimedia Mail Meeting
sections.content:
On July 23-24, 1984, representatives from four major computer research organizations met at Bolt Beranek and Newman to discuss the experimental multimedia mail system. Multimedia mail lets people send messages containing not just text, but graphics, images, voice and structured data like spreadsheets. The meeting brought together developers from BBN, the Information Sciences Institute (ISI), Stanford Research Institute (SRI), and Linkabit to share what they had built and agree on standards for future work.

BBN's Diamond system could already handle compound documents with text, graphics, images, voice and spreadsheets on the Jericho workstation, and was being ported to the Sun. ISI was building a new user interface on Xerox workstations. SRI had a multimedia mail system on Sun workstations with text, voice and graphics support. Each group was solving similar problems independently, creating a need for common technical agreements.
sections.plainLanguage: People from four organizations who were all building email for pictures and sound met to share what they had done and decide how to do things the same way.

sections.title: Standardizing Multimedia Syntax and Graphics
sections.content:
The groups agreed to adopt a revised syntax for multimedia mail messages, moving away from the informal approaches each group had developed. All groups committed to switching over to this new syntax by October 1, 1984, with updates to RFC 767 to document it.

For graphics representation, the group examined two established standards (ACM-CORE and GKS) but found they lacked good support for grouping graphical objects together and for storing graphics in standard file formats. BBN had developed an interim protocol for graphics in the Diamond system (documented in MMM-18 and MMM-23). The group agreed to adopt this as the MMGraphics1 protocol as an interim standard while monitoring the development of the GKS standard, with a goal to eventually settle on an adopted international standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The groups agreed on a common way to write multimedia messages and how to represent drawings, and said they would switch to it by October.

sections.title: Document Presentation and Media Types
sections.content:
A key challenge was how to represent documents with different sizes, resolutions and fonts across display devices. The group agreed to develop a method for recording the author's intent regarding presentation, deferring final decisions to the reader's document presenter. This would handle grouping objects, font attributes (like bold and italic), headings, and sections, while avoiding the rigid page boundaries and absolute positioning that formal document systems used.

The group also discussed new content types beyond text, voice and images. BBN presented a spreadsheet/chart media type that transmitted both the data and the spreadsheet model, letting readers change values and see effects on the conclusions. Future ideas included animated graphics (line drawings with temporal information) and forms (sets of name-value pairs for collecting information). All systems agreed to gracefully handle unknown media types by displaying a message like 'An object of type X appears here' rather than crashing.
sections.plainLanguage: They decided documents should adapt to different screen sizes instead of forcing a fixed layout, and talked about supporting new types of content like spreadsheets and animations.

sections.title: The MPM Protocol and Wider Adoption
sections.content:
The Multimedia Protocol (MPM) was the message transport mechanism enabling multimedia mail systems to communicate. The group planned to have two implementations ready by end of summer: on TOPS-20 computers at ISI and on Sun workstations at SRI, BBN and other sites. This would allow regular use of multimedia mail across the Internet with the goal of testing realistic multi-hop message routing.

To encourage wider use and test interoperability, the group discussed adding MPM to SMTP translation, allowing multimedia messages to be converted to text-only mail that older systems could read. BBN already had an Import/Export component doing translations in both directions. They also agreed to add support for a Float64 data type (64-bit IEEE standard floating point) to the data representation format specified in RFC 759, and to include an optional text Caption property on all object types for labeling non-visual content and providing fallbacks when media types were not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: They set up a way for different computers to send multimedia mail to each other and agreed on how to convert it to old-style plain text email when needed.

sections.title: Agreements and Next Steps
sections.content:
The meeting produced a concrete list of further actions with assigned people and due dates. Key items included revising RFC 759 and RFC 767 by September 1, documenting document presentation semantics by October 1, completing the Sun Workstation MPM implementation by September 15, and acquiring GKS standard documentation. A mailing list for multimedia mail discussions was set up at ISI (MMM-People@USC-ISIF.ARPA).

The group planned a follow-up demonstration in January 1985 to show the revised multimedia syntax, graphics objects alongside text, images and voice, document presentation semantics in action, and the Sun Workstation MPMs operating together. This would demonstrate not just individual features but real multi-system interoperability of a working multimedia mail network.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone agreed on what to do next and when to do it, and planned to test everything together in January.
